issues.legal_issue: Land does not vest in a planning authority merely because it is shown as required by a town planning scheme when it was not lawfully acquired.
material_facts: The planning records and an unchallenged arbitrator’s award identified the disputed strip as private land held for the owners of adjoining plots.
The planning authority was entered as the owner of the strip in the scheme records, but the authorities produced no evidence of acquisition, purchase, or lawful taking of possession.
The authorities admitted that the strip had never been acquired, and no compensation had been paid to its owners.
issues.conclusion: The strip did not vest in the planning authority; the scheme’s entry alone could not deprive its owners of the land.
issues.legal_principle: Article 300-A of the Constitution prohibits deprivation of property except by authority of law. Section 88 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 must be read with sections 59, 65, 66, 125 and 126, rather than in isolation. Sections 125 and 126 provide for acquisition and compensation, while sections 65 and 66 protect owners’ interests. The Court relied on Vimlaben Ajitbhai Patel v. Vatslaben Ashokbhai Patel, State of Bihar v. Project Uchcha Vidya, Jelubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat, Bishambhar Dayal Chandra Mohan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra, Wazir Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh, and K.T. Plantation Private Limited v. State of Karnataka.

rule.if: town_planning_scheme_case and land_was_privately_owned and land_was_not_acquired and no_compensation_was_paid

predicates.town_planning_scheme_case: The dispute concerned whether land vested in a planning authority through a town planning scheme.
predicates.land_was_privately_owned: Records and an arbitrator’s award identified private persons as the owners or holders of the land.
predicates.land_was_not_acquired: The authority did not acquire, purchase, or lawfully take possession of the land.
predicates.no_compensation_was_paid: The authority paid no compensation to the private owners for the land.

issues.definition: When a town planning scheme concerns land shown by the records to be privately owned, but the authority neither acquires it nor pays compensation, the land does not vest in that authority.

issues.legal_issue: Correcting an erroneous entry that identifies a public authority as owner of private land is not a substantial variation of a town planning scheme.
material_facts: Property records and the arbitrator’s award identified the disputed strip as private land held by the owners of adjoining plots.
The scheme records later identified the planning authority as the owner, although the authority had not acquired the strip and its own records acknowledged that it had not taken possession.
The correction sought was to remove the authority’s name as owner; the strip was a private road, not a public road.
The authority rejected the proposed correction on the mistaken premise that it owned the land and that deletion would remove a public road.
issues.conclusion: Removing the authority’s erroneous ownership entry was a correction of an error, not a substantial variation; the scheme was to be modified to record the legitimate owners.
issues.legal_principle: Section 91 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 permits variation where a scheme is defective because of an error, irregularity, or informality, if the variation required is not substantial. Correcting the record to reflect the true ownership of a private road does not convert a public road into a private one or constitute a substantial variation. The Court also relied on sections 64, 65 and 73 concerning ownership particulars, changes to plots, and the finality of an arbitrator’s decision.

predicates.administrative_refusal_to_correct_planni: A public authority refused a request to correct an ownership entry in a planning record.
predicates.ownership_records_identified_private_own: The relevant ownership records identified private persons as the owners or holders of the land.
predicates.planning_record_identified_authority_as_: A planning record identified a public authority as owner despite the ownership records identifying private owners.
predicates.the_land_was_a_private_road: The disputed land was recorded and treated as a private road rather than a public road.

issues.definition: When a public authority refuses to correct its erroneous ownership entry for a private road despite records identifying private owners, the entry must be corrected as a non-substantial scheme variation.

issues.legal_issue: A planning authority cannot undo an unchallenged, final arbitrator’s award by making an inconsistent ownership entry in the scheme records.
material_facts: An arbitrator’s award identified the disputed strip as a private road held for the owners of the adjoining plots, consistently with the property records.
The award was not challenged by the planning authority or the owners.
A later scheme record identified the planning authority as owner, without evidence of a procedure that transferred ownership to it.
issues.conclusion: The arbitrator’s award was final and binding, and the planning authority could not undo it through an inconsistent entry in the scheme records.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 72 and 73 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 govern the arbitrator’s role and the finality of the arbitrator’s decisions. The Court distinguished Laxminarayan R. Bhattad v. State of Maharashtra, where the scheme and an award providing compensation for the land were materially different, and noted that the award in Pukhrajmal Sagarmal Lunkad v. Municipal Council, Jalgaon concerned a different statutory context and facts.

rule.if: town_planning_scheme_case and arbitrator_award_determined_ownership and award_was_not_challenged and later_scheme_entry_conflicted_with_award

predicates.town_planning_scheme_case: The dispute concerned ownership recorded through a town planning scheme.
predicates.arbitrator_award_determined_ownership: An arbitrator issued an award identifying who owned or held the disputed land.
predicates.award_was_not_challenged: The affected authority and owners did not challenge the arbitrator’s award.
predicates.later_scheme_entry_conflicted_with_award: A later entry in the scheme records identified ownership inconsistently with the award.

issues.definition: If an unchallenged award determines ownership and a later scheme entry conflicts with it, the planning authority must follow the award.

issues.legal_issue: A writ court may enforce a public duty by mandamus where a public authority wrongly exercises its discretion, and disputed facts do not automatically bar relief when they can be determined from the record.
material_facts: The owners sought correction of the planning records and challenged the authority’s refusal in a writ proceeding.
The relevant ownership documents and arbitrator’s award supported the owners’ claim, and the authorities admitted that the private road had not been acquired.
The refusal relied on an incorrect ownership premise and gave vague reasons for alleged non-compliance with legal requirements.
The parties had litigated for many years, and the Court considered a remand for a new hearing unnecessary.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition; the authorities were directed to correct the records and carry out the necessary consequential changes.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, mandamus may enforce a legal right and corresponding public duty where a public authority fails to perform that duty or exercises its discretion unlawfully. Disputed questions of fact do not by themselves require a writ court to refuse jurisdiction where the issues can appropriately be resolved on the evidence, including documentary evidence. The Court relied on Directors of Settlements v. M.R. Apparao, Gunwant Kaur v. Municipal Committee, Bhatinda, State of Kerala v. M.K. Jose, and ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. It also exercised its power under Article 142 to direct complete relief.

predicates.writ_proceeding_seeks_enforcement_of_pub: A person brought a writ proceeding seeking performance of a duty by a public authority.
predicates.applicant_has_legal_right: The applicant held a legal right that the authority’s performance would protect.
predicates.authority_failed_or_wrongly_exercised_it: The public authority failed to perform its duty or exercised its discretion on an incorrect or irrelevant basis.
predicates.material_facts_can_be_resolved_from_the_: The material factual issues could be determined from the record without requiring the court to refuse writ jurisdiction.

issues.definition: A writ court may compel a public authority to perform its duty when the applicant has a legal right, the authority has failed or acted wrongly, and the material facts can be resolved from the record.
